Al-Samani summarises the same meaning briefly. Ibn Kathir and others take the giving of life to include the resurrection, and death to refer to the end of life in this world. Al-Razi offers a wider reading: God alone has the exclusive ability to create life and death, with no obstacle or opponent able to prevent it, and he sees in this a rational proof of God's oneness. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that the two verbs may be read as a predicate of an implied subject or as a circumstantial clause; al-Nasafi accepts both readings. Ibn 'Ashur observes that mentioning life and death recalls the doctrine of resurrection, which the polytheists denied, and shows that their idols have no power over either. Ibn Sa'di sums up that God is the Creator, Provider and Governor of all things by His power.

This verse states that God is the First, before whom nothing exists, the Last, after whom nothing remains, the Manifest, above whom there is nothing, and the Hidden, nearer to everything than anything is to itself, and that His knowledge encompasses all things. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the First and the Last mean eternity and permanence after the perishing of creation, that the Manifest means exalted and dominant, and that the Hidden means encompassing and near, citing the hadith of Abu Hurayra recited at bedtime. Ibn Abbas, as relayed by al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi, reads the Manifest as the one who prevails and the Hidden as the one who knows what is inward, an interpretation al-Razi attributes to al-Zajjaj. Al-Sam'ani, al-Nasafi and Ibn Atiyya hold that the Manifest is known through evidence and the Hidden is beyond the senses, a view Ibn Juzayy also prefers. Al-Razi develops the notion of priority by linking it to necessary existence, while Ibn al-Qayyim argues that these four names do not contradict one another and that the conjunctions join them to show their totality. All agree on God's complete knowledge. Commentators also debate what the conjunctions between these names convey, notably al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi, and some apply the verse to the believer's doubts, as Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn Abbas. The shared conclusion is that God unites these perfections and nothing escapes Him.

This verse states that God created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne in a manner befitting His majesty. He knows what enters the earth, such as seed, rain and the dead, what comes out of it, such as plants and minerals, what descends from heaven, such as rain, angels, provision and decrees, and what ascends to it, such as angels and human deeds. He is with you wherever you are, and His sight sees your deeds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy read these attributes as God's knowledge, power and all-encompassing dominion. Most commentators take the six days as days of this world, while al-Hasan notes that God could have created everything in an instant. As for His being "with" you, Ibn Abbas, al-Thawri and Ahmad ibn Hanbal, as well as al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, understand it as His knowledge and power, and al-Qurtubi says the scholars agreed on this reading. Ibn Kathir, quoting Ibn Taymiyya, adds that the general sense of the word "with" does not imply mixing of essences. Al-Hasan affirms this presence without specifying how. Regarding istiwa', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as rising above, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and others refer back to the discussion in Surat al-A'raf, and Ibn Ashur sees it as an image of sovereignty. Modern commentators such as Sayyid Qutb and Ibn Uthaymin stress the spiritual lesson and the apparent sense of the text, without settling the questions of modality.

This part of the verse states that God alone owns the heavens and the earth entirely, and that all matters return to Him. Al-Tabari explains that His authority is binding over everything in them and that the affairs of all creatures lead back to Him, who will judge among them by His wisdom. The commentators agree on this exclusive sovereignty and on the return to God on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir adds that He owns both this world and the next, judging with justice and never wronging anyone, even by the weight of an atom. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the word 'affairs' here covers all existing things, both their attributes and their substances, whereas Ibn 'Ashur understands it as human actions and the persons themselves, who will be recompensed. The common reading is 'turja'u' with a u vowel, while al-Hasan, al-A'raj and others read 'tarji'u'. Al-Qurtubi takes the repetition of the sovereignty as emphasis. Nearby verses, according to al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, speak of a presence of knowledge and power rather than of place. No legal ruling appears in this passage.

This verse states that God makes part of the hours of the night enter the day, lengthening the day, and makes part of the hours of the day enter the night, lengthening the night, and that He knows what the hearts conceal. Al-Tabari explains this as the alternation of the length of day and night, and reports from 'Ikrima and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i that winter days are shortened by the lengthening of the night, and summer nights are shortened by the lengthening of the day. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin stress that this gradual change follows divine wisdom and that no creature can do it except God. As for the closing phrase about knowing what the breasts hold, the commentators agree that it means the complete knowledge of God, who knows the intentions, secrets and inner thoughts even when people themselves are not fully aware of them.

Most read the verse as a call to reflect on God's control over time. Ibn 'Ashur sees in it a refutation of the pagan belief that time, the succession of night and day, is what destroys human beings, while al-Razi discusses why the power of God is mentioned before His knowledge. Al-Qurtubi notes that the repetition of the phrase about God's dominion over the heavens and earth serves to emphasise the point. Ibn Kathir explains that the presence of God mentioned in the previous verse refers to His knowledge and watchfulness rather than physical nearness, and al-Razi reports that theologians understand it as either knowledge or protection.

Al-Jaza'iri and al-Nasafi summarise these meanings, and Ibn 'Ashur notes that the names of God mentioned at the start of the surah, including the All-Knowing and the Governor, are numerous, while commentators differ on whether the surah is Meccan or Medinan.

The verse calls believers to stand firm in faith in Allah and His Messenger and to spend from the wealth of which He has made them trustees. Commentators explain that wealth truly belongs to Allah, and people hold it only as stewards or deputies; whoever believes and gives will receive a great reward. They agree that the spending meant includes obligatory zakat as well as voluntary charity, and that a person should hasten to give before the wealth leaves him. On the meaning of istikhlaf, Mujahid takes it as being granted provision and long life, al-Hasan as inheriting wealth from earlier generations, and others as the duty to fulfil the rights attached to property. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note that the verse may have been revealed concerning the expedition of Tabuk, and that the phrase about those who believed and spent was said by some to refer to Uthman, while others hold its ruling is general. The verse then rebukes those who refuse to believe though the reasons are present, namely the Prophet's call and the covenant taken. Scholars differ on this covenant: Mujahid and al-Tabari take it as the pledge made in the loins of Adam, whereas others understand it as the proofs God placed in human reason. Ibn Uthaymin reads the particle min as explanatory, leaving the believer to give as the interest requires.

God rebukes those who refuse to believe when every reason for belief is present: the Messenger calls them to believe in their Lord, and God has already taken their covenant. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Mujahid understood this covenant as the one taken from the descendants of Adam when they were made to testify that God is their Lord. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi explained it as the proofs God placed in human reason and the capacity to reflect that He gave to people. Ibn Kathir also connected it with the pledge of allegiance made to the Prophet, while al-Razi considered the first interpretation weak, since people know of that primordial covenant only through the Prophet's word. On the reading, al-Tabari held that the common reading (akhadha, with mithaqakum in the accusative) and Abu 'Amr's reading (ukhidha, with mithaqukum in the nominative) are close in meaning, preferring the former as more widely transmitted. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi take the address as a call to the believers to remain steadfast, whereas most commentators address those who have not yet believed. Al-Tabari reads the conditional clause as meaning that if you ever wished to believe, now is the most fitting time. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as affirming the natural disposition to faith placed in human nature, so that rejecting it is stubbornness.

This verse says that God sends down clear signs to His servant Muhammad ﷺ, which most commentators identify as the Qur'an (al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi), while some include the miracles in general (al-Qurtubi, al-Alusi). Its purpose is to bring people out of darkness into light. All agree that darkness stands for disbelief and polytheism and light for faith. Al-Tabari quotes Mujahid, who describes the passage as moving from misguidance to guidance.

The commentators agree that the verse closes by stressing God's kindness and mercy towards His creatures, and that guidance is itself a mercy. They differ, however, on who performs the bringing out. Al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan note that it may be God through the Qur'an, or the Messenger through his call, and both readings are accepted. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy stress that the signs are proofs that remove doubt. Al-Razi rejects the idea that God creates faith in people, reading the verb as a gentle favour (lutf). Al-Shinqiti, relying on Surah al-Talaq, explains that the call is addressed to all, but the actual coming out of darkness is granted only to those whom God guides.

Ibn 'Ashur distinguishes ra'fa, aversion to harm, from rahma, the wish for good. Al-Sha'rawi uses the same contrast: the first removes pain, the second protects from relapse. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi also note two accepted readings of the word ra'uf, with and without the extended vowel.

This verse urges believers to spend in the way of God. It asks them what prevents them from doing so, since God inherits the heavens and the earth and all that is in them: whatever is in their hands will ultimately return to Him, so it is better to spend what they still possess. The commentators agree that the spending and fighting meant here are those done in the way of God, and that the verse ranks those who spent and fought before the conquest above those who did so afterwards. All agree that God promised both groups the good reward, which is Paradise, with differing degrees. On the identity of the conquest, the majority view, reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Zayd ibn Aslam, Mujahid and al-Kalbi, is the conquest of Mecca. Al-Sha'bi and al-Zuhri hold that it is the treaty of Hudaybiyya, a view al-Tabari prefers on the basis of a hadith transmitted from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. Ibn Kathir notes that the verse may have been revealed before the event, as a foretelling of what would come. Several commentators report that it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, the first to embrace Islam and the first to spend for God's cause. They cite the Prophet's words: 'Do not revile my companions; if one of you spent the equivalent of Uhud in gold, he would not reach the mudd of one of them nor half of it', to stress the greatness of the early believers' merit. Some explain that spending in times of weakness is harder and therefore more meritorious, since the need was greater. The verse also encourages the generous loan to God, which commentators interpret in several ways: spending in the way of God, maintaining one's family, increasing acts of worship, or simply any good deed.

This verse calls on believers to spend in the cause of God, describing the charity as a loan made to God, a comparison with a loan that is repaid with more. The plain meaning is that whoever gives from his wealth, with a willing heart and sincerely for God, will receive from his Lord a multiplied reward, and besides it a noble recompense, which the commentators identify as Paradise. They agree that the beautiful loan is a sincere expenditure made for God's sake, and that the multiplication may reach seven hundred times or more. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi take the spending in God's cause as the intended subject, and al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi explain that the noble reward means Paradise. The meaning of the beautiful loan, however, is disputed: al-Mawardi reports from al-Hasan that it means voluntary acts of worship, from Zayd ibn Aslam that it means spending on one's family, from Muqatil ibn Hayyan that it means spending in God's cause, and others that it means simply saying glory be to God and praise be to God. Al-Qurtubi and al-Qushayri, like al-Razi, list conditions for a good charity: lawful income, choosing the best of one's wealth, sincerity free of display, no reproach or harm, and discretion. Ibn Kathir holds that the term covers any sincere gift. The occasion of revelation is also reported: Abu al-Dahdah gave his orchard after hearing it, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr reports Jews who mocked the verse. Al-Razi finally holds that the spending meant includes both the obligatory and the voluntary.

This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when the believing men and women will see their light running before them and on their right, and they will be given the good news of gardens beneath which rivers flow, where they will abide forever, which is the great triumph. The commentators agree on the general meaning but differ on the nature of this light. The majority, including Ibn Mas'ud and Qatada as reported by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, understand it as a real light, varying in brightness according to deeds, some shining only as far as their feet. Al-Dahhak, and al-Tabari after him, take it to mean guidance and faith, with the books given in the right hand. Ibn 'Atiyya notes both readings, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that the blessed receive their records from these two directions, making the light a sign of their status. On the preposition in the phrase on their right, al-Farra' and al-Tabari read it as meaning in or from, while others read it as on. Most hold that the angels speak the good news, meaning entry into the gardens. The hypocrites then ask the believers to let them share their light; they are told to go back and seek light elsewhere, and a wall with a gate is set between them, its inner side holding mercy and its outer side punishment. Ibn Zayd identifies it with the A'raf, al-Hasan and Qatada describe a barrier between paradise and hell, while others link it to the wall of Jerusalem, a view Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan consider weak. The believers rebuke them for corrupting themselves, waiting, doubting and being deceived by false hopes and by Satan, and no ransom will be accepted from them; the Fire will be their abode.

This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when the hypocrite men and women say to the believers: "Wait for us, that we may borrow some of your light." The commentators explain that believers receive a light in proportion to their deeds, by which they walk across the bridge, while the hypocrites either receive a deceptive light that is later taken from them, or receive none and must borrow from others. On the word unzurūnā, most explain it as "wait for us," since the believers are hurried toward Paradise; Hamza's reading anzirūnā means "grant us respite." Al-Tabari judged the connected reading to be the more correct. As for the speaker of "return behind you," Ibn 'Abbas attributes it to the believers, while Qatada and Muqatil attribute it to the angels; it is a rebuke and a mockery. Some take it to mean returning to the place where the light was distributed, others returning to worldly life to earn faith and good deeds. A wall with a gate is then set up between them, its inner side holding mercy and its outer side punishment. The scholars agree it is a barrier between Paradise and Hell, but differ on its identity: Mujahid links it to the partition of al-A'raf, Qatada describes it as a wall between the two abodes, and reports attributed to 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr and 'Ubada place it at the eastern wall of the Jerusalem mosque, a view Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur do not accept. The hypocrites ask, "Were we not with you?" They are answered: "Yes, but you led yourselves into temptation, you waited for misfortune to befall the believers, you doubted, and false hopes deceived you until the command of Allah came; and the Deceiver deceived you."

This verse depicts the Day of Resurrection, when a wall is set between the believers and the hypocrites. The hypocrites call out to the believers: "Were we not with you?" The believers reply that they were with them only outwardly, that they destroyed themselves through hypocrisy and temptation, waited for misfortune to strike the believers, doubted, and were deceived by false hopes until God's command came, and that the Deceiver deceived them. The commentators agree that "being with them" meant sharing outward acts such as prayer, fighting and other worship, and that hypocrisy was hidden disbelief that ruined its holders. They differ on some terms. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take the waiting as delaying repentance or awaiting calamities for the believers, while Mujahid and Ibn Zayd explain the doubt as scepticism about God, His oneness and prophethood; Muqatil and Ibn Kathir also mention that the waiting could mean awaiting the Prophet's death. The "false hopes" are, for Qatada, the snares of Satan; for Ibn 'Abbas, worldly life; for Abu Sinan, saying "we will be forgiven"; and for others, simply long expectations. Most identify the Deceiver as Satan, and some read the word with a vowel change. Most take "God's command" to mean death, though Qatada understands it as their being cast into the Fire and Ibn 'Abbas as the triumph of Islam. Ibn Kathir notes that reports linking this wall to Jerusalem contain Israelite material, and that the wall is a barrier set on the Last Day.

The verse states that on the Day of Judgment no ransom will be accepted from the hypocrites or from those who disbelieved, that their refuge is the Fire, which is their most fitting abode, and that it is a dreadful destination. The commentators explain that this is said to the hypocrites once they have been separated from the believers, and that fidya means anything one might offer to ransom oneself, whether wealth or otherwise. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that the denial covers both hypocrites and disbelievers. Most take the word mawlakum to mean "more deserving of you". Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as "protector", meaning they have no helper except the Fire. Al-Razi holds that faith and repentance are included in fidya, so no repentance will be accepted that day. The reading with ya is the most common, while Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read it with ta'. The commentaries also mention the light given to believers and taken from hypocrites, and the wall set between them. Qatada and Ibn Kathir understand it as a barrier between Paradise and Hell, while some place it at Jerusalem, a view Ibn Kathir considers unreliable.

This verse calls believers to let their hearts grow humble and soft at the remembrance of God and at hearing the truth revealed, and not to become like those who received the Scripture before them: after a long time passed, their hearts hardened and most of them became defiant. The commentators agree that humility of the heart (khushu') means submitting and obeying God's command and prohibition, and that the rebuke here is a gentle call rather than a scolding. They report, through Ibn Mas'ud, that only four years passed between their conversion and this admonition, while Ibn 'Abbas places it thirteen years after the start of revelation. Several occasions of revelation are mentioned, such as excessive joking and laughter, or requests for stories addressed to Salman al-Farisi. On who is addressed, al-Kalbi and Muqatil see the hypocrites, while Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and al-Qasim b. Muhammad see the believers of this community, and Muqatil b. Hayyan sees the believers among the People of the Book. On the word 'amad', Mujahid renders it as 'the long duration', Ibn Hibban as 'distant hope', and others as the length of life, the wait for victory, or the wait for the Last Day. Most conclude that the One who revives the earth with rain can also soften hearts hardened by neglect, through the remembrance and the Qur'an.

In this verse God declares that He brings the dead earth back to life after it has dried up, and this is offered as an image of how He revives hearts hardened by neglect through remembrance and admonition. He has made the signs clear so that people may reason. The commentators differ on how far this image should be taken. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi, al-Baghawi and others keep to the apparent sense: rain brings the plants back to life, and this is compared to the return of hearts to faith and fear of God. Ibn Juzayy judges the literal meaning the more evident and sound. Others, such as al-Razi, read it as a proof of God's power to raise the dead. On the figurative sense, Salih al-Murri and Ja'far al-Sadiq explain that reviving means softening hearts after their hardening, or restoring justice after injustice.

Most exegetes connect the verse to what precedes it, where God rebukes the believers for being slow to humble their hearts at the remembrance, and warns them against imitating the People of the Book whose hearts hardened over a long time. The reports cited, from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, place this rebuke four years or thirteen years after the revelation began, and mention causes such as joking or the weariness of the companions. The commentators cite these reports without deciding between them.

All agree on the closing sense: God has made His signs clear so that you may reason and understand.

This verse states that men and women who give charity and make a goodly loan to God will have their reward multiplied and will also receive a generous reward, which the commentators identify as Paradise. Al-Tabari holds that both readings, the doubled sad of al-mutasaddiqin and the single sad of al-musaddiqin, are correct in meaning, and he takes the goodly loan to mean spending in God's cause, a view shared by al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that a goodly loan is giving from good wealth, with a willing heart and sincere intention, to someone who deserves it. Al-Sam'ani lists further conditions: the wealth must be lawful, given without reminders or harm, chosen from the best of one's possessions. The commentators agree that the multiplication ranges from ten times up to seven hundred times, as Ibn Kathir reports, and that the generous reward is Paradise. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan note that linking a verb to a noun inside the relative clause is acceptable because the participle carries a verbal sense, though others see a grammatical difficulty and propose different analyses. Many exegetes connect this passage to the following mention of the truthful and the martyrs. Ibn 'Abbas, Masruq and al-Dahhak take them as separate categories, whereas Mujahid and Ibn Mas'ud hold that every believer is truthful and a martyr, and others take martyrs to mean prophets or those slain in God's cause. The commentators do not settle between these views and simply report the arguments behind each.

This verse states that those who believe in Allah and His messengers are the truthful (al-siddiqun), that the martyrs have their reward and their light with their Lord, and that those who disbelieve and deny Our signs are the companions of the blazing fire. The commentators differ on how the sentence is structured. Ibn 'Abbas, Masruq, al-Dahhak and Abu al-Duha hold that the sentence ends at “they are the truthful”, and that “the martyrs” begin a new statement about particular martyrs, so the truthful and the martyrs are distinct groups; some understand these martyrs as those slain in the cause of Allah, others as prophets who bear witness against their peoples. Mujahid, Ibn Mas'ud and Zayd ibn Aslam instead join “the martyrs” to what precedes by a conjunction, holding that every believer is truthful and a witness. Al-Tabari prefers the separate reading, arguing that faith alone does not ordinarily make someone a martyr in common usage. As for “truthful”, Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas take it to mean every believer in Allah and His messengers, while al-Dahhak and Muqatil take it to mean those who believed the messengers without denying them even briefly, such as the believer of Pharaoh's household, and in this community eight men who embraced Islam first, with 'Umar joining them. On the light, most commentators take it literally, a light walking before them on the Day of Resurrection, whereas Mujahid understands it as guidance, honour and glad tidings. The verse follows the call to spend in the way of Allah, whose givers will be repaid.

This verse describes the worldly life as play, diversion, adornment, boasting among people, and competition in wealth and children, all of which are fleeting. The commentators read it as a call to belittle this world and to give greater weight to the Hereafter. Qatada explains that play and diversion mean eating and drinking, while Mujahid says every play is diversion; others distinguish between what makes one desire this world (play) and what distracts from the Hereafter (diversion). Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi offer further readings of boasting and multiplication: pride may rest on physical strength, lineage or family, whereas the believers' increase lies in faith and good deeds. The image of rain and plants shows how quickly worldly life passes: the crop delights the eye, then yellows and crumbles. Scholars differ on the word al-kuffar. Ibn Mas'ud and others take it to mean farmers, who cover the seed with soil, while many others take it to mean disbelievers, who are more attached to worldly goods. The Hereafter brings a severe punishment for God's enemies and forgiveness and good pleasure for the obedient. Some commentators read the punishment and the forgiveness as alternatives for those who chose this world or the next. The overall conclusion is that worldly life is a deceptive enjoyment for one who clings to it and forgets the Hereafter, but a provision that leads to God's pleasure for one who uses it toward that end, as Sa'id ibn Jubayr said.

This verse calls believers to race toward forgiveness from their Lord and toward a garden whose breadth is like the breadth of the heavens and the earth, prepared for those who believe in God and His messengers. It is a bounty from God, given to whom He wills, and God is the Possessor of great bounty. The commentators explain that this racing is done through the deeds that earn forgiveness. Al-Kalbi and al-Nasafi understand it as repentance, Makhul as being in the first takbir with the imam, others as the first row in battle, and Ibn Juzayy notes that these are examples while the general meaning covers all good deeds.

Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari, agree that mentioning the width without the length conveys vastness, and that the heavens and the earth refer to their kind. Ibn Kathir links the verse to the brevity of worldly life and cites the hadith that a whip's place in Paradise is better than this world and all it contains.

Opinions differ on whether Paradise already exists. Al-Razi, Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn Kathir take the verb 'was prepared' as evidence that it is created now, while Ibn 'Atiyya reports the view without settling it, and Ibn 'Ashur holds that the verse does not decide the matter. Al-Razi also lists several interpretations of the comparison, including the view of Ibn 'Abbas that it refers to one of several gardens.

On the relation between grace and deeds, al-Razi, following the majority of Sunni scholars, holds that Paradise is pure grace rather than something earned, while al-Qadi replies that grace and merit can coexist. Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi stress that entry is only by God's mercy and bounty.

This verse states that every affliction striking the earth or the self, whether drought, failed harvests, illness or bereavement, is recorded in the Preserved Tablet before it was created, and that this is easy for God. Commentators differ on what the pronoun in 'before We bring it into being' refers to: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, among others, take it mainly to mean the souls, while others refer it to the earth or to the affliction, and Ibn Kathir considers it best to extend it to all creation, a view Ibn al-Qayyim also adopts. On the meaning of 'affliction', Ibn 'Abbas and others take it broadly as any good or evil, whereas Ibn Juzayy, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur mostly understand it as harm in its ordinary sense. All agree that the 'Book' is the Preserved Tablet. The stated purpose is that people should not grieve over what escapes them nor exult arrogantly in what they receive. Ibn 'Abbas holds that the believer turns hardship into patience and blessing into gratitude, a view Ikrima also reports. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur add that the blameworthy grief is the kind that drives one away from patience and submission, while ordinary sorrow joined with acceptance is permissible. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the verse also comforts believers and encourages trust in God, while not discouraging effort. The passage continues by condemning arrogance and stinginess.

The verse explains that every calamity striking the earth or the self is recorded in the Preserved Tablet before creation, so that believers neither grieve excessively over what escapes them nor rejoice arrogantly in what Allah gives them. The commentators agree that grief should lead to patience and joy to gratitude. Ibn 'Abbas and Ikrima note that everyone experiences sorrow and joy, but the believer turns hardship into patience and blessing into thanks. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim stress that this decree is settled in advance, and that remembering it calms the heart.

Opinions differ on the calamities meant. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid take them as drought, lost harvests, illness, death and lack of sustenance, while Muqatil also includes the enforcement of legal penalties and Ibn Jurayj the narrowness of livelihood. On the pronoun in "nabra'aha", the view reported is that it refers to the souls, to the earth, or to the calamity, and Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Qurtubi prefer that it covers all of creation. Al-Razi, presenting the Sunni and Mu'tazili arguments, discusses at length how this decree relates to human free will.

Regarding the reading of "atakum", Abu 'Amr reads it short, meaning "came to you", while most readers read it long, meaning "gave you". Al-Tabari considers both correct and prefers the long form, whereas Abu 'Ubayd favours the short one. The commentators clarify that the blamed joy is the kind that leads to conceit and boasting, not joy that is accompanied by gratitude, as Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi observe.

This verse states that God does not love those who are stingy with what they owe and who urge others to be stingy. It adds that whoever turns away from obedience, such as by refusing to spend in God's cause, harms only himself, because God is self-sufficient and alone deserves praise. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand stinginess as refusing to pay God's due from wealth, while Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di also see it as encouraging others to be stingy by word and example. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya extend the meaning to wealth, status and knowledge. Al-Sam'ani notes that generosity is the pleasure of giving and stinginess the pleasure of withholding. Sa'id ibn Jubayr reads it as withholding knowledge, and al-Suddi and al-Kalbi relate that it refers to Jewish scholars who hid the description of the Prophet. Ibn 'Ashur identifies these people as hypocrites who discouraged spending on believers. Scholars also differ on the reading: Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir omit the word huwa, and al-Tabari holds that both readings are correct. Grammarians differ on how to parse the opening relative pronoun, taking it as a substitute, as a subject with an implied predicate, or as a qualifier. The surrounding verses speak of destiny and divine wisdom, which some commentators connect to the warning against stinginess.

The commentators explain that God sent His messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Book containing the laws and the balance, meaning justice, so that people might stand upright in fairness. They agree that the Book refers to the scriptures in general. Most take the balance to mean justice, as Qatada and Mujahid did, and Ibn Kathir describes it as the truth that sound reason confirms. On the sending down of iron, opinions differ. Ibn 'Abbas and others report that Adam came down from Paradise carrying iron tools, whereas al-Hasan, Qutrub, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari take the descent to mean the creation and provision of the metal, as is said of livestock. All agree that iron holds great might, which is used to make weapons, and great benefit for crafts and daily life. Regarding the phrase 'that God may know who helps Him', al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya clarify that it refers to knowledge made manifest in events, not to a new divine knowledge, since God knows all things eternally. Ibn 'Abbas explains that the helpers support Him without seeing Him. Ibn Sa'di links the Book and the iron, proof and sword, as the means by which the religion is upheld. The commentators conclude that God is strong and mighty and needs no help from anyone, but He has charged His servants with supporting Him so that they may benefit and be rewarded.

This verse tells us that God sent Noah and Abraham and placed prophethood and the Book among their descendants. Among those descendants some were guided, but most of them turned away from obedience to God. Most commentators understand the Book as the revealed scriptures, though Ibn 'Abbas explains it as writing with the pen. They agree that the one who is guided is the one who followed the messengers, and that the wrongdoers are those who departed from obedience. On the meaning of disobedience, Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil take it as disbelief or sin, while al-Razi distinguishes the grave sinner from the unbeliever. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari hold that the wrongdoers are the majority. Ibn 'Ashur links the verse to the deviation of Arab polytheists and Jews from the path of Noah and Abraham. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite reports about people abandoning the truth after Jesus and inventing monasticism, which explain the following verse. Others simply recall the history of earlier nations without further detail.

This verse recounts that God sent a succession of messengers after Noah and Abraham, culminating in Jesus, son of Mary, to whom He gave the Gospel. He placed compassion and mercy in the hearts of his followers. It then speaks of the monasticism they invented, which God had not prescribed for them, but which they adopted seeking God's pleasure. Most commentators agree that they did not observe it as it should have been observed, yet they differ on who failed to keep it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that it was those who came after the innovators, who had altered their religion, while Ibn Zayd and Ibn 'Atiyya argue that the original founders themselves did not persist in it. Qatada explains that the monasticism meant renouncing women and taking to hermitages, and al-Mawardi adds withdrawal to the deserts and mountains. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya read the exception as disjunctive and compare the failure to a broken vow. Al-Razi also holds that the believers mentioned are those who believed in Muhammad, and the defiant ones are those who rejected him. Ibn Kathir and others report traditions about the origin of this practice, whose authenticity is debated. The verse ends with a double reward for those who believed in Jesus and then in Muhammad, which several commentators link to narrations transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas.

God addresses the believers, commanding them to fear Him and to believe in His Messenger, and promises them two portions of His mercy, a light by which they will walk, and forgiveness. The commentators differ on who is addressed. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak, followed by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, understand it as the believers among the People of the Book who first believed in Jesus and then in Muhammad, and who thus receive two rewards, as the hadith of Abu Musa about the man of the People of the Book who is given his reward twice seems to confirm. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others take it as addressed to all believers of this community. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn 'Uthaymin lean towards believers in Muhammad, who receive a reward equal to that of believing People of the Book, while al-Shinqiti holds that this community's reward is even greater. On the meaning of the two portions, Ibn Zayd speaks of the reward of this world and the next, others of the reward for secret and public deeds, and others of fulfilling the rights of God and the rights of people. As for the light, Ibn 'Abbas takes it to be the Qur'an and Mujahid guidance; al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari see it as the light on the Day of Resurrection by which believers walk over the bridge, and al-Razi and al-Nasafi connect it with the light mentioned in the verse 'their light runs before them'. Ibn al-Qayyim notes that only light makes walking profitable. On the phrase 'so that the People of the Book may know', the majority reads the 'la' as superfluous, meaning that the People of the Book should know they have no share in God's bounty. According to Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari, the verse answers the boasting of the People of the Book over the Muslims, while Qatada says it answers their envy.

This verse states that God grants those who believed in Moses and Jesus and who also believe in Muhammad ﷺ two portions of His mercy, a light to walk by, and forgiveness, and then gives the purpose: that the People of the Book who did not believe should know that they hold no share of God's bounty, since bounty is in God's hand and He gives it to whom He wills. The commentators broadly agree that the opening address is to the People of the Book who believed in their messengers, that the bounty refers to what the believers in Muhammad ﷺ receive, and that the verse was revealed in response to envy or boasting that arose between the People of the Book and the Muslims, as Qatada and Ibn Abbas report. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the two portions as two rewards, one for faith in the earlier prophet and one for faith in Muhammad ﷺ, with Ibn Kathir citing Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who speaks of a double reward. Ibn Zayd holds that the two portions are the reward of this world and of the next, while others see one as the reward for avoiding sins and the other for doing good deeds. On the light, Ibn Abbas identifies it with the Quran, Mujahid with guidance, and others with the light that will guide on the bridge on the Day of Judgment. Regarding the particle la in li-allā, most exegetes treat it as superfluous, while Abu Muslim al-Isfahani and al-Razi read it as a negation and refer the pronoun to the Prophet and the believers. Some identify the bounty with prophethood, with Islam, with provision, or with innumerable blessings. The verse closes by affirming that God is the possessor of great bounty.
